title: Sergeant York, 1918 — the man who didn't want to fight captured 132
sources: Wikipedia: Alvin York — Tennessee farmer and blacksmith; after a 1915 religious conversion, his church opposed all forms of violence; 'I didn't want to go and kill because I believed in my Bible'; on his draft registration he wrote 'Yes. Don't Want To Fight.'; his conscientious objector claim was denied and he was drafted; persuaded by his commanders through Bible passages; on 8 October 1918, in the Meuse–Argonne offensive near Hill 223 and Chatel-Chéhéry, 17 men were sent behind German lines to silence machine guns; machine-gun fire killed six Americans and wounded three; York fought the machine guns — 'I didn't want to kill any more than I had to. But it was they or I.'; a German officer emptied his pistol at York without hitting him, then offered to surrender; York and seven men marched back 132 prisoners; General Lindsey: 'Well York, I hear you have captured the whole German army.' York: 'No sir. I got only 132.'; promoted to sergeant, awarded the Medal of Honor; refused many offers to profit from his fame

Also on this day (candidates.md / Wikipedia On This Day): 1829 Stephenson's Rocket won the Rainhill Trials; 1871 the Great Chicago Fire began; 1956 Don Larsen threw the only perfect game in World Series history

Archive film (public domain / CC0, Wikimedia Commons): 'Draft and Mobilization Activities 1917-1918' (US draft lottery); 'Filming the American Attack at Château-Thierry' (US Signal Corps, July 1918 — illustrative of US troops in France, not York's own action)

Photos (public domain): York's conscientious objector claim of appeal; Sgt. York, 1919; York home in Tennessee, 1919; 328th Infantry line of advance, Hill 223, 7 October 1918 (Signal Corps); Frank Schoonover's 1919 painting of York's action; the valley near Chatel-Chéhéry

post.facebook:
On this day in 1918, Alvin York captured 132 German soldiers in the Argonne Forest.

York was a farmer and blacksmith from Tennessee, and his church opposed all violence. On his draft registration he wrote: "Don't want to fight." He was drafted anyway, and his officers argued with him, Bible in hand, until he agreed to serve.

On 8 October 1918, German machine guns pinned down his battalion. Seventeen men were sent behind the German lines; six were killed. York kept firing — "I didn't want to kill any more than I had to," he said later. A German officer emptied his pistol at him and missed, then offered to surrender. York and seven men marched back with 132 prisoners.

"Well York, I hear you have captured the whole German army," his general said. York replied: "No sir. I got only 132." He received the Medal of Honor.

Also on 8 October: Stephenson's Rocket won the Rainhill Trials (1829), and the Great Chicago Fire began (1871).
